terms.definition: The first stage of the pathway: an endocrine gland detects a trigger and releases a hormone directly into the bloodstream.
terms.function: Synthesizes and stores a specific hormone, then releases it into nearby blood vessels in response to an internal trigger, such as a nerve signal, a change in blood chemistry, or another hormone.
terms.whereItIs: At the gland — the leftmost group in the model, where the small ring at its base pulses each time it releases.
terms.whyItMatters: This is where a hormone message begins — without release into the bloodstream, the rest of the chain has nothing to carry.

terms.definition: The second stage: the released hormone travels through the blood, passing by cells throughout the body until it reaches ones that can respond to it.
terms.function: The circulatory system carries the hormone molecule from the gland to every part of the body, exposing it to far more cells than the few that will actually respond.
terms.whereItIs: Along the curved vessel connecting the gland to the target cell, where small traveling hormone particles are visible mid-flow.
terms.whyItMatters: Because the bloodstream reaches everywhere, one gland's release can influence tissues far from where the hormone was made — but only where a matching receptor exists.

terms.definition: The third stage: a hormone binds to a receptor on a target cell whose shape matches it, like a key fitting a lock.
terms.function: The receptor protein's shape matches only its specific hormone; binding triggers a shape change in the receptor that starts a signal cascade inside the cell.
terms.whereItIs: At the tip of the small receptor protruding from the target cell's membrane, facing the incoming vessel.
terms.whyItMatters: This matching step is why a hormone can pass right by most cells with no effect — only the cells built to recognize it respond at all.

terms.definition: The fourth stage: binding at the receptor sets off a chain of changes inside the target cell, changing what the cell does.
terms.function: The bound receptor activates internal signaling molecules that alter the cell's behavior, such as turning specific genes on or off, or speeding up an existing process.
terms.whereItIs: At the internal marker near the center of the target cell, visible when the cross-section cutaway is active.
terms.whyItMatters: This is the actual payoff of the whole pathway — everything before it (release, travel, binding) exists only to trigger this change inside the cell.

terms.definition: The fifth stage: the body senses the cell's response and signals the gland to adjust hormone release up or down to stay balanced.
terms.function: A sensor — often the gland itself, or a controlling structure like the pituitary gland — detects the resulting change and signals the gland to increase or decrease further hormone release, keeping the response within a healthy range.
terms.whereItIs: Along the thin dashed arc that loops from the target cell back over the scene to the gland.
terms.whyItMatters: Feedback is why hormone levels settle back to normal instead of overshooting — it's the body's built-in way of self-correcting, and it's what breaks down in conditions like diabetes.

terms.definition: A chemical messenger made by a gland that travels through the blood and changes how a target cell behaves.
terms.function: Carries a specific instruction from the gland that made it to any cell in the body that carries a matching receptor.
terms.whereItIs: Produced inside a gland, then released into and carried by the bloodstream.
terms.whyItMatters: Hormones are the actual 'message' in hormone signaling — without a hormone molecule, there's nothing for the bloodstream to carry or a receptor to bind.

terms.definition: An organ that makes and releases hormones directly into the bloodstream, such as the pancreas or thyroid.
terms.function: Synthesizes a specific hormone and secretes it into nearby blood vessels when triggered.
terms.whereItIs: Located throughout the body; real examples include the pituitary, thyroid, adrenal glands, and pancreas, mapped in the Human Anatomy branch's Endocrine System unit.
terms.whyItMatters: Glands are the source of every hormone signal — this model's single generic gland stands in for the whole set of real endocrine glands.

terms.definition: The network of blood vessels that carries hormones from the gland that made them to cells all over the body.
terms.function: Provides a body-wide transport route so a hormone made in one gland can reach target cells anywhere.
terms.whereItIs: The circulatory system as a whole; in this model, represented by a single vessel segment running from gland to target cell.
terms.whyItMatters: Without the bloodstream's constant circulation, a hormone would have no way to reach a target cell that isn't right next to the gland.

terms.definition: A protein on or inside a cell shaped to bind one specific hormone, like a lock built for a particular key.
terms.function: Recognizes and binds only its matching hormone, converting that binding event into an internal signal the cell can act on.
terms.whereItIs: On the surface (or inside) of a target cell — in this model, the small protrusion on the target cell facing the vessel.
terms.whyItMatters: The receptor is what makes a cell a 'target' at all — no matching receptor means no response, no matter how much hormone passes by.

terms.definition: A cell that has the matching receptor for a hormone, so it's the one cell type that actually responds to that hormone's message.
terms.function: Receives the hormone signal via its matching receptor and changes its behavior in response.
terms.whereItIs: Wherever a matching receptor exists; in this model, the single large cell on the right side of the scene.
terms.whyItMatters: Different hormones have different target cells — this is how one bloodstream carrying many hormones can produce many different, specific effects around the body.

terms.definition: A control system where the result of a hormone's action sends a signal back to the gland to increase or decrease further hormone release.
terms.function: Keeps hormone levels within a healthy range by adjusting future release based on the outcome of past release.
terms.whereItIs: Conceptually spans the whole pathway; in this model, shown as the dashed arc looping from the target cell back to the gland.
terms.whyItMatters: Feedback loops are what keep the endocrine system self-correcting rather than constantly over- or under-shooting — the mechanism behind homeostasis for hormone levels.

terms.definition: The whole network of glands throughout the body that produce and release hormones.
terms.function: Coordinates slower, longer-lasting body-wide processes — growth, metabolism, blood sugar, stress response — by releasing hormones into the blood.
terms.whereItIs: Made up of glands distributed throughout the body, mapped as anatomical structures in the Human Anatomy branch's Endocrine System unit.
terms.whyItMatters: Hormone signaling is the process the endocrine system as a whole carries out — this component shows the general pathway; the Endocrine System unit shows where the real glands sit in the body.
